title: Surtsey: An Island Born from the Sea
context:
In November 1963, the crew of a fishing boat off the south coast of Iceland noticed smoke rising from the sea and the smell of sulphur. An undersea volcano was erupting, and within days a new island had appeared. Named Surtsey after the fire giant Surtr of Norse legend, it continued to grow for almost four years, until the eruptions stopped in 1967. At its largest, the island covered about 2.7 square kilometres. Its surface remained too hot to walk on for months afterwards, and steam still escaped from cracks in the cooling rock.

Almost at once, scientists recognised an extraordinary opportunity. Unlike most places on Earth, Surtsey had been born sterile, because the heat of the lava killed every living thing. Whatever arrived later would have come from elsewhere, and researchers could record the process of colonisation from the very beginning. To keep the experiment pure, the Icelandic government declared the island a protected reserve, and since then only a handful of scientists have been permitted to land there. Even they must wash their clothing and check their boots for seeds before they arrive.

The first colonists were microorganisms and simple plants. Bacteria and fungi appeared in the volcanic ash within months, and in 1965 the first flowering plant, a sea rocket, was found growing on the beach. Its seeds had been carried by ocean currents. Mosses and lichens followed, and about a decade later seagulls began nesting on the island. The birds proved decisive: their droppings fertilised the thin soil, allowing grasses and many other plants to take root where nothing could have survived before. Today more than seventy species of flowering plants have been recorded, although not all of them have lasted.

Animal life has also arrived. Insects were carried on the wind or on floating debris, and spiders sailed in on silk threads. Seals now breed on the beaches, and puffins have started to nest in burrows on the grassy slopes. Meanwhile, the island itself is shrinking. Waves and storms have eaten away the soft volcanic ash, and the surface area has halved. Geologists predict that within a few more centuries only the hard rock core will remain above the sea. Divers have also noted that kelp forests and fish have gradually established themselves around the island, completing a picture of a new ecosystem.

The scientific significance of Surtsey was recognised in 2008, when UNESCO placed it on the World Heritage List. Researchers say that the island offers lessons for conservation, because it shows how quickly ecosystems can form without human interference, and how important a single factor, such as the arrival of seabirds, can be. It also gives a preview of how life might establish itself on newly exposed land when glaciers retreat, a process that is becoming more common as the climate warms.
